BIOCOLOOP: COLLABORATIVE AGENTIC RESEARCH
FOR BIOLOGICAL MODEL IMPROVEMENT
Anonymous authors
Paper under double-blind review
ABSTRACT
Biological data are often distributed across institutions and data holders, where
privacy and data-sharing constraints limit centralized access. A key challenge for
self-improving AI in this setting is to use such distributed evidence to improve
both model parameters and the computational solutions built around them. Col-
laborative learning typically optimizes fixed models, whereas automated model
design and research generally rely on centralized training and evaluation signals.
Bridging the two is nontrivial: distributed evidence must support not only opti-
mization, but also the evaluation and refinement of computational changes that
generalize beyond their local settings. To tackle this, we introduce BioCoLoop, a
collaborative research framework that couples client-local parameter fitting with an
evidence-guided proposal–evaluation loop. Local training shards update a shared
predictor, while local development shards produce aggregate evidence cards that
guide the next executable proposal. Across three biological settings spanning drug–
target interaction prediction, observed-response proteomics, and cell perturbation,
we evaluate BioCoLoop with ten simulated laboratories against single-laboratory
fixed-model and direct-optimization baselines. The complete system achieves the
highest score on four of five evaluated endpoints. BioCoLoop offers a practical
path toward self-improving biological AI under data-sharing constraints.
1. INTRODUCTION
Biological laboratories generate valuable measurements for predicting molecular interactions, pro-
tein responses and cellular perturbations. Privacy and data-sharing constraints often require these
measurements to remain at their original institutions (Sheller et al., 2020; Bakhtiari et al., 2025).
How can laboratories use their collective experimental evidence to improve a predictor while retain-
ing their own data? Beyond fitting shared parameters, we aim to automate a second part of model
development: choosing and revising prediction components and training configurations using feed-
back from participating laboratories. This calls for a collaborative research process in which local
evidence informs both model training and the next design experiment.
Figure 1 contrasts two complementary approaches. A centralized research agent iterates on data
accessible to its execution environment, using experiment outcomes to revise candidate solutions.
AIDE and the AI Scientist automate this process for computational research (Jiang et al., 2025b; Lu
et al., 2024); DrugEvolve applies algorithm revision, evaluation and memory to drug-development
tasks (Zhou et al., 2026; GAIR-NLP DrugEvolve contributors, 2026). These workflows turn mea-
surements into design feedback. Collaborative learning instead connects several data holders through
local training and model-update aggregation (McMahan et al., 2017; Sheller et al., 2020; Wang et al.,
2024). Here, a client is a laboratory’s computational worker, which operates on data held by that
laboratory. This approach broadens the evidence available for fitting a specified model. Connecting
the two requires a second shared interface: laboratories must also evaluate candidate designs and
supply feedback that the research agent can use to choose its next experiment.
BioCoLoop couples these interfaces in a two-level research cycle. For any candidate design, an inner
training process fits a shared predictor using laboratory-local data. An outer research loop uses the
resulting development evidence to propose and select subsequent designs. We define an executable
design by its trainable prediction components and its learning-rate, regularization and aggregation
settings. These choices let the loop adapt how a predictor learns while keeping the biological task

Our contributions are threefold. First, we connect laboratory-local parameter fitting to distributed
evaluation of executable model designs through a common biological research interface. Second, we
develop an evidence-guided loop mechanism that packages proposal outcomes into reusable research
history and uses measured learning trajectories to select candidates for further validation. Third, we
evaluate BioCoLoop across the three task families above. Controlled comparisons separate the effects
of laboratory participation, proposal feedback and training-budget allocation. We also examine how
performance changes with the research model, the number of participating laboratories, additional
independent datasets and the number of research iterations.

3. METHOD: COLLABORATIVE AGENTIC BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH
3.1 FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
BioCoLoop takes a task specification, an initial predictor, an editable design space and data held by
K participating laboratories. The task specification defines prediction inputs and outputs, scorer and
computational budget. Each laboratory maintains training and development partitions. A research
controller proposes a design, a shared training service fits its parameters across laboratories, and
local evaluators return development measurements to a coordinator. The outputs are the selected
design with fitted parameters and an ordered history of proposals and outcomes (Figure 2).
The key mechanism is the return of experimental evidence to the research process. An evidence card
links a proposed change to its executed configuration, aggregate learning trajectory and selection out-
come. Successive cards form a persistent history, allowing the controller to revise its next hypothesis
using both successful and unsuccessful trials. Trajectory information also guides training allocation:
a candidate with promising early progress can be promoted for full validation. The outer loop decides
what design to investigate and how to allocate evaluation; the inner process fits parameters for that
design.
3.2 EVIDENCE-GUIDED PROPOSAL AND REVISION
The controller receives the task specification, current design and accumulated evidence cards. It
returns a structured proposal with four fields: a hypothesis stating why a change should help, an
experiment describing the comparison, an expected_effect identifying the predicted metric or
diagnostic response, and a design_id resolving to an executable configuration. A validator checks
the identifier against the task’s editable design space. The configuration determines the intervention;
the other fields state its rationale and anticipated outcome. Appendix A gives the JSON schema and
design library.
Local evaluators return scores, losses and learning-curve diagnostics. The coordinator packages these
with the proposal, selected checkpoint and acceptance decision. It retains a candidate if its mean
development score exceeds the incumbent’s, using lower mean loss to resolve ties. Each subsequent
proposal receives the complete evidence history, including rejected directions. The research language
model remains fixed; adaptation occurs in the predictive model and the designs explored by the loop.
Evidence influences two research decisions. In proposal revision, measured history conditions the
next design. In training allocation, short learning trajectories determine which designs receive full
validation. The latter uses a screening–promotion–validation policy that retains candidates with
strong current scores as well as improving trajectories. These decisions share the evidence inter-
face and are evaluated separately: proposal-history comparisons assess design selection, while fixed-

4.2 DRUG–TARGET INTERACTION PREDICTION
DTI predicts a binary interaction from a compound and a protein sequence. We use the released
BindingDB training/development split of 50,149/5,604 pairs. Canonical-compound groups are as-
signed to clients with a label-independent size-balancing rule, producing compound-disjoint clients
while preserving the source split within each client.
The task reference uses the released TAPB architecture with frozen public ESM2 protein features
and freshly initialized drug, fusion and classification modules (Lin et al., 2025). A target dictionary
derived from client 0’s training proteins is shared identically by every arm, ensuring a common
initialization. The objective combines TAPB’s classification NLL and masked-language loss under
the shared batch-64 training pipeline. Candidate designs can add a zero-output residual adapter
before TAPB’s native confounder-averaged prediction.
Selection uses mean-client AUROC; AP, MCC, accuracy at 0.5 and binary cross-entropy are sec-
ondary. The fixed test suite contains 5,505 random, 3,791 unseen-drug and 2,507 unseen-protein

4.3 PROTEOMICS-BASED EFFICACY PREDICTION
We construct an observed-response eﬀicacy benchmark from a subset of the public ProteinTalks
PTPC supplement, which provides measured proteomic responses and binary eﬀicacy labels (Sun
et al., 2026). The task predicts eﬀicacy from a treated condition’s observed 6h/24h proteome and
drug representation. We partition the 491-condition source pool, spanning 333 compounds, into
386 fitting and 105 development conditions by compound group. Ten clients each own 49–50 total
conditions, with compound-disjoint training and development groups and both classes in every local
development set. Local fitting sets contain 35–42 conditions.
The task reference is a ProteinTalks-derived observed-response eﬀicacy head: protein and drug con-
volutional branches followed by a 64–32–1 classifier, trained from random initialization on observed
6h/24h responses and Morgan features. A 24h linear/Morgan model provides a complementary non-
neural reference.
Average precision (AP) is primary; AUROC, binary cross-entropy and accuracy at 0.5 are secondary.
The 148-condition test role is evaluated after the development-selected checkpoint is frozen.
4.4 CELL PERTURBATION IDENTIFICATION
Given an observed expression response and five candidate interventions, the model selects the true
perturbation by cosine agreement with predicted responses. We construct three inverse-identification
benchmarks: VCC-derived single-gene perturbations from the public 2025 training release with inter-
nal intervention-disjoint partitions (Arc Institute, 2025); Norman double-gene overexpression (Nor-
man et al., 2019); and a Tahoe-100M subset of 307 compounds in A549 at 5 µM, from the February
25, 2025 release (Zhang et al., 2025). Whole-intervention train/development/test counts are respec-
tively 60/20/20, 70/20/27 and 180/60/67. Each laboratory owns six/seven/eighteen training interven-
tions and two/two/six development interventions. Assignment balances intervention identities, while
retaining the naturally varying number of VCC cells per intervention.
The public CELLxGENE-pretrained scDEBART backbone is frozen and its response MLP is train-
able (Sung & Kim, 2026). Three upstream attention masks are implemented as additive blocking
masks and verified by response-free synthetic tests. This correction leaves pretrained weights, tar-
gets, splits and candidate rosters unchanged; features are then re-extracted for every arm.
Genetic tasks use the released perturbation encoding and exclude directly perturbed genes from loss
and ranking coordinates. Tahoe adds fixed Morgan-projection conditioning for chemical identities.
The uniform cell objective combines response MSE with 0.1 times a contrastive loss formed from
local training conditions.
Primary scoring is intervention-macro Top-1, with a 20% random-choice expectation; micro Top-1,
MRR, Top-3 and cosine-logit cross-entropy are secondary. All arms receive the same five candidate
interventions for each response.

6. CONCLUSION
BioCoLoop connects laboratory-local parameter fitting to an evidence-guided research loop through
shared proposal, training and evaluation interfaces. The complete system leads four of five main-
comparison endpoints, and compute-matched allocation improves Norman Top-1 by 10.84 points
on average. Independent-source experiments demonstrate transfer gains from selected DTI and cel-
lular collections, while laboratory-count and dual-proposer studies identify the effects of partition-
ing, source compatibility and research budget. The results distinguish parameter-learning gains, eﬀi-
cient allocation and proposal-history effects, providing an empirical basis for collaborative biological
model development and more effective research feedback.

Proteomic preprocessing.
For each 6h and 24h profile, the PTPC adapter applies log1p, within-
profile min–max normalization over finite observations, zero filling and unit L2 normalization. The
2,048-bit Morgan vector is separately L2-normalized and scaled by 0.5. Concatenating the two 5,171-
dimensional proteomic blocks with the drug vector produces a 12,390-dimensional float32 input. The
ProteinTalks-derived eﬀicacy head contains 464,193 parameters at D00. Every arm uses identical
inputs, initialization policy, 100-round budget and checkpoint rule.
